Manuscript: IFP transcript 1059, copied from a manuscript belonging to G. Swaminatha Gurukkal of Tiruvadudurai. MS L No. 154a. Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0, February 13, 2009.
Country of Publication: India || The Greatness of the Śivāgamas and Other Scriptures ||
Homage to the Bindu, the eternal one,
and to the Guru, the Lord of the Gaṇas.
Some, relying on the view of the non-theists (*nirīśvaravādins*), [assert] that the Smṛtis possess authority because they are uncreated,
whereas the Śiva-Āgamas lack authority because they are created; even if they do possess it in some way, it is for humans who have fallen from the path of the Vedas— thus say those of evil intellect.
The Lord spoke all that web of texts beginning with the Vedas.

And because of the Pauṣkara-Śivāgama scripture which states: "From the invisible, tranquil Śiva, the supreme cause, that which has the form of sound (nāda) has emerged; [from that] everything exists."

Furthermore, the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) are: phonetics, ritual, grammar, etymology, metrics, and astronomy; along with Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya-vistara, the Purāṇas, and the Dharmaśāstras—these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge.
Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda—following this sequence, the science of weapons (Astrashastra) is supreme; thus, eighteen sciences are traditionally recorded.
Of these eighteen sciences, which follow divergent paths:
The scripture states that the original author is the poet Śūlapāṇi himself;
thus, the eighteen Purāṇas have been described in brief.
Among their various creations, in the Dvāpara age,
the sage Vyāsa appeared as Mahādeva, the revealer of the Kāmika and other scriptures.
Just as the Lord Maheśvara is the author of the divisions beginning with the Kāmika, so too is the son of Satyavatī the author of the eighteen Purāṇas.
Thus, just as the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, Dharma-saṃhitā, and Sūta-saṃhitā possess authority because they were composed by Śiva himself along with the Śrutis such as the Kāmika,
so too [the Agamas] possess authority because they were composed by Vyāsa, who is an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa; yet even so, this [Agama] remains distinct.

And from the *Sūtasamhitā*’s response: the authority of the Vedas and the Śiva-āgamas rests solely on their being composed by the supremely trustworthy Paraśiva, not on their being uncreated. This is because they possess the arrangement of phonemes, words, and sentences, like the speech of Kālidāsa and others. Thus, the Vedas are [authoritative] as effects produced by a cause.

If it is argued that they are eternal, then so too are the Śiva-āgamas, because of the scriptural statement: "The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being. Thus, Śiva’s status as the agent of manifestation is established; or rather, let his uncreatedness be accepted.
This has been stated in the Sūta-saṃhitā:
The Veda is beginningless, and Śiva is its manifestor in the ultimate sense;
it is only with reference to this manifestation that the wise call it "praṇava."

Likewise, in the *Sahasranāmavyākhyā*, regarding the term *kṛtāgamāya*, it is said: "He by whom the Āgamas—the specific Tantras such as the *Kāraṇakāmika* and others—have been composed or produced, is *kṛtāgama*.
Thus it has been stated.

"From the *Kāmika* up to the *Vātula*, these are the Śiva-āgamas spoken by Śiva," thus explained Alaṅkāra-dīkṣita. Therefore, the authority of both [the Vedas and the Āgamas] rests precisely on their being composed by Śiva. This has been stated in the *Caturvedārthatātparya-saṃgraha*:
Even while asserting that "the Vedas are the authority," people understand your divine scripture as their very life-breath;
for it is through the categories of meaning suitable for the subject matter of the words concerning meditation upon you that [this is known].
And up to the root, having assumed a physical form.
If the Kalpas have been composed by us sages as authoritative, O Great Sage,
why is it not possible for us great sages to state that those [other views] are corrupted by partiality? What authority do we have over the great sages?
Other tantras maintain that Śiva is their author.
And in the Vāyavyasaṃhitā:
"By Śiva, who is omniscient and free from all defects whatsoever;
therefore, the words of the Lord are to be trusted by the wise."
According to the reality of their merits and demerits, one who lacks faith in them goes downward.
(p. 4) Therefore, rather than being mutually complementary like the Vedas, both possess authority as independent entities. As it is said in the *Mataṅga*:
"The word of the Lord is the sole authority; it is the truth."
In the Pauṣkara as well:
"The word of that [Lord] is the sole authority; it is true and an eternal treasure of the highest good. This has likewise been explained by the venerable Vidyāraṇya in the Sūtasaṃhitā.
In the procedure for the worship of Śiva:
"O best of the twice-born, there is both Vedic and Tantric [worship];
however, that which is Tantric belongs only to the Tantrika and not to anyone else, while the Vedic belongs only to the Vaidika."

In this context, the Vedic method is that which is set forth in the Vedas, the Smṛtis, the Purāṇas, and so forth, which are rooted in them; the Tantric method is that which is set forth in the Āgamas such as the Kāmika, spoken by Śiva and independent of those [Vedic sources]. Regarding these, he states the specific qualification for the Tantric method with the words: "only for the Tantric practitioner."

The meaning is that [this applies] only to one who has been consecrated by the initiatory rites (*dīkṣā*) and so forth, preceded by the construction of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the mandala, and other such requirements. For instance,
it is not the case that the independent Śiva-āgamas are mutually [contradictory] like the Vedas.

It is not outside the Veda (*vedabāhyatvam*). This Tantra is the essence of the Veda, for it is declared to be a specific excellence of the Veda, superior even to the Vedas themselves. As it is stated in the *Vāyavyasaṃhitā* of the *Śaiva Purāṇa*:
"O Blessed One, we wish to hear that which was expounded by Śiva."
p. 5) "The knowledge of Śiva is the essence of the Vedas for those who have heard it, leading to liberation. And in the Makuṭa [Tantra]:
"This Tantra is the essence of the Vedas; therefore, one who follows the Vedic path should practice it."
This knowledge, consisting of the meaning of Vedānta, is the supreme and auspicious final doctrine.
The twenty-eighth tantra, arising from the *ūrdhvasrotas*, is to be known as the most excellent;
it bestows the essential meaning of the Vedas, whereas others are merely means for achieving different purposes.
In the *Suprabheda*: "The Śaiva, Pāśupata, Soma, and Lākula systems are fourfold.
Among these, the Śaiva is supreme and gentle, while the Pāśupata and others are fierce."
The twenty-eight tantras beginning with the Kāmika are known as Śaiva;
that very same [tradition] is declared to be the Saumya, and indeed that alone is the Siddhānta.
"Other than that, the Raudra Tantra, such as the Pāśupata and others, has been described.
And in the Kāmika:
'The Siddhānta is the essence of the Vedas; other [systems] are excluded from the Vedas.'"
In the established doctrine, the conduct prescribed therein is called Vedic conduct.
Whatever is to be done should be performed provided it is not in conflict with Śaiva rites;
if it is in conflict, it should be abandoned, but one must never abandon what is Śaiva.
All that is Vedic which is not in contradiction with the words of Śiva is to be accepted;
indeed, the Śaiva is said to be the Vedic, and the Vedic is the Śaiva itself.
The Śaiva [tradition] is both internal to and external to the Vedic; that [Vedic tradition] is also below it.
Nevertheless, the Śaiva is superior to the Vedic, for there is nothing higher than it.

The Siddhānta consists of the Kāmika and other scriptures; there is nothing higher or more supreme than this. The Śaiva [tradition] is indeed the fundamental source, and from it the four Vedas have arisen.

Nevertheless, O lords of sages, because its meaning is identical [to the Vedas], the Śaiva tradition is declared everywhere to be Vedic and the essence of the Vedas, according to such statements as "tathāpi vaidikam" and "vedasāram."
Now, is it not the case that one Tantra is the essence of the Vedas, based on Śruti, and dependent;
while another Tantra, such as the Kāmika and others, is not the essence of the Vedas, is not based on Śruti, and is independent?
This has been stated in the Vāyavya-saṃhitā:
The Śaiva Āgama is also traditionally held to be of two kinds: the Śrauta and the Aśrauta.
The Śrauta is considered to consist of the essence of the Vedas (Śruti), while the other is regarded as independent.
The independent [Tantra] was first tenfold, and then eighteenfold;
established under the names beginning with *Kāmika*, it is designated as the Siddhānta.
But there is another [work] consisting of the essence of the Vedas, with an extent of one hundred crores [of verses],
wherein the supreme Pāśupata vow and knowledge are expounded.
This being the case, how is it stated in the *Makuṭa* and other texts that the *Kāmika* and other [Tantras] constitute the essence of the Veda?

This is true. There are two ways in which the status of being the essence of the Veda is established as being "Vedic" (*śrauta*). Among these, the first [way] consists of the hundreds of millions of [Tantras] that elaborate upon the objects of knowledge of the Vedic Pāśupatas, as perceived within the Śaiva and Pāśupata Tantras.
In detail, in a certain [work] today (p.
7), up to the point where it is seen that the eight Siddhas possess independence therein, as well as the essence of the Veda and conformity with the Veda.

The detailed exposition of categories and other subjects that expand upon the objects of knowledge in the second Siddhānta is seen in the independent tantras such as the Kāmika; however, its being the essence of the Vedas does not mean it has arisen from the Veda like butter from curds, but rather that it conforms to the Veda.

Or, it is the state of being pervaded by the Vedas; or something else has also been stated. "Conformity with the Vedas" means the acceptance of the meaning of the Vedas, because [the Purāṇa] truly pervades the Vedas. As it is said in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:
As it has been said: "Whatever exists otherwise in other scriptures is found in the Śiva-āgama;
whatever is not seen in the knowledge of Śiva does not exist elsewhere."
And in the Kāmika:
"The firm conclusion of the scripture is that there is no knowledge higher than the Siddhānta; otherwise, it would be so among the [other] Āgamas."
"The twenty-eight tantras are proclaimed as the Siddhānta. And in the Cintyaviśva:
"The Śaiva and Pāśupata are to be known as the sole leaders of all principles (tattvas)."
It should be known as consisting of all mantras, and it shall consist of all deities.
"And the arising of knowledge of the true path through austerities performed in other births.
And in the *Aruṇācala-māhātmya*: "There is no sacred field greater than Śoṇādri; there is no mantra greater than the five-syllabled one."
There is no dharma superior to that of Maheśvara, and there is no scripture superior to the Śivāgama.
However, because contradiction with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is inherently rooted in contradiction with the object of cognition (*prameya*), there exists,

as in the case of the Vedas, a mutual contradiction in some respects and in certain places regarding the modes of presenting portions of objects of cognition such as the doctrine of a single self (*ekātmavāda*).
By not abandoning the [Vedic] suffixes (*mātra*), by being free from the deficiency of contradicting the injunctions and prohibitions ordained in the Vedas,
and by accepting the meaning of the Vedas through non-contradiction— since there is frequently identity of purpose— with the conduct prescribed in the Vedas,
[the author] refers to those "learned in the Śaiva-Veda" with independence, as established in the *Suprabheda*.

The ultimate meaning is that the essence of the Veda consists precisely in the Śiva-veda named Śivāgama, which possesses the specific quality of being a Veda that reveals meanings both already known and unknown through the Vedas—
just as the status of being a Brāhmaṇa is a specific quality of humanity that produces humans.
As it is said in the *Mokṣakārikās*:
"Since that [knowledge] which has been set forth for the purpose of opposing the fetters and false views does not lose its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
all fetters are here [rendered ineffective] by it in every respect."
Nor does that [scriptural injunction] subvert their validity within their own respective domains;
for in those [domains], the conduct prescribed by caste and stage of life is not like that [scriptural injunction], which is based on direct authorization.

Nor is its object obstructed by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, even for one who has transcended delusion (*viśoka*), action must be preceded by the impulsion of the Lord (*pati*). And in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
The Purāṇa is established by the Vedas and the Āgamas, which contain its declarations;
it consists of both general and specific Śaiva speech that possesses distinct characteristics.
And in the *Vṛddhācalamāhātmya*:
"These, indeed, are the forms of the Supreme Lord [installed] in the pavilions of the temple of Vṛddhācaleśa."
Having established [the images] in their respective places, he performed worship according to the specific methods taught in the Śiva Āgamas.

Furthermore, the distinction here is this: being outside the Veda (*vedabāhyatva*) consists precisely in propounding meanings that are in many respects contrary to the Vedas, not in every respect. For if it were so [in every respect], then all other scriptures, such as those of the Cārvākas and others, as well as the Śaiva scriptures, would also [be considered outside the Veda].
Since there exists, in some way or another, the capacity to convey even contradictory meanings, it is not the case that [these means] are entirely external;
rather, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are indeed fruitful according to their respective nature. As it has been said in the Śivāgama and in the work composed by the Guru:

The Cārvākas [hold that the self] is perfected from the elements; the Smārtas [hold it to be] in the collection of the subtle elements (tanmātra); the Vaiśeṣikas [hold it to be] in the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); and the Mānasas hold it to be in the sense organs as well.
The Buddhists are established in the principle of consciousness (*buddhi-tattva*), while the Naiyāyikas are established in that which is not the true principle.
The Arhats abide in the quality (guṇa), the Pāñcarātrikas in the principle (tattva), and the Vedāntins, Sāṃkhyas, and Yogins in the primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa).
The Śaiva Paurāṇikas are established in Rāga; the Somas are established in the stage of Vidyā; the Kāpālas, however, are intent upon Kalā; and the Kāleśvaras are established in Kāla.
The Pāśupatas [are established] in Māyā, while those of the Great Vow are in Vidyā.

Those who belong to the Pravāheśvara [tradition] are indeed those for whom Īśa is the instigating agent (*prayojyakartṛ*). Those who abide in the principle of Sadāśiva are called Śaivas, as they proclaim their connection with Śiva;
those in Śakti are Śāktas, and those in Śiva are remembered by the wise as Sāmānya (Common).
The proponent of the Siddhānta maintains that liberation consists in attaining union with Śiva (*śivasāyujya*).
This very state of union with Śiva is described as follows: "Liberation is the severance of the name; here, liberation is not the identity of the bound soul (*paśu*) and Śiva."
"There is neither the destruction of ignorance by being swallowed up, nor the dissolution of the qualities (guṇas), nor liberation from the state of a stone;

rather, that nature of the Self which is of the form of consciousness and bliss, manifested upon the departure of the three impurities—that is declared to be 'union' (sāyujya). In the Śaiva Tantra, liberation is the omnipresent Lord who is identical to Śiva. Thus [it is said].

Therefore, it is established even without stating that the Śiva-śāstra is superior to general Ṛṣi-sūtras and other scriptures simply because it was composed by Śiva himself, who is directly established as a Great Sage (maharṣi) through the authority of the Vedas. Consequently,
in the Sūta-saṃhitā and other texts—
The dharma arising from the upward flow is superior to the dharma arising from the downward flow;
the Smārta dharma is greater than the dharma arising from the upward flow.
"O best of sages, the Vedic (srauta) duties are superior to those based on tradition (smārta).
Although in some instances the meaning may have been stated otherwise, that statement is sublated by the pure Great Saying (mahāvākya) of Śiva.
The superiority of the Śiva-Āgama over the Veda is established by the scriptural testimony of its origination from the mouth of Īśāna.
As it is said in the *Śrīmaddhālāsyamāhātmya*: "O Brahmins, the divine Śiva-knowledges, such as the *Kārikās* and others,
emerge from the upper face of the venerable Lord Hālāsya."
Furthermore, from the mouth of the God of gods known as Puruṣa,
he proclaimed the Ṛgveda, which consists of twenty-one divisions.
And on the right [he holds] the Yajurveda with its one hundred and one branches, while on the left [he holds] the Sāmaveda together with its thousand divisions.
"He spoke the Atharvaveda, divided into nine parts, by means of Sadyojāta.
And in the Śrīkāmika:
"From the mouth of Īśāna, situated above, [he spoke] the letters beginning with 'ka'..."
The Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva [Vedas] arose from the Puruṣa... [and so forth].
The Siddhānta, Gāruḍa, Vāma, Bhūtatantra, and Bhairava.

"Respectively facing upward, eastward, northward, Kubera’s direction (north-east), southward, and downward. Therefore, among all the scriptures— such as those of the Cārvākas and the Śaiva Siddhāntins— which were composed by either the supreme Self who is authoritative or by both [the supreme Self and other authorities], [this is the most excellent].
Just as in the case of the means of valid cognition such as perception, by virtue of their respective capacities to cognize objects already known or not yet known,

there exists a relationship characterized by the sublated and the sublator, the general and the particular, the pervaded and the pervader, the incidental definition (*taṭastha-lakṣaṇa*), and the essential definition (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*).

The validity of means of knowledge—whether limited or unlimited by the object to be proven—is established. Indeed, no single means of knowledge is valid for one of sound mind. For if that were accepted: "If Sugata is omniscient, what proof is there that Kapila is not? (p. 12)

Furthermore, since it is impossible to explain how there could be a difference of opinion between two omniscient beings, it would follow that all scriptures are invalid, resulting in the undesirable consequence of universal blindness for the world.
Therefore, all scriptures are indeed authoritative within their own respective limits; this has been established accordingly.
This has been stated by the venerable Śivācārya Rāmakaṇṭha in the *Rauravavṛttiviveka*,
and it is also said in the *Pauṣkara*:
"There is yet another path, such as that of the Vedas and so forth, which reveals the meaning of the fetters of the bound souls (*paśu*)."
"The pervasion up to the limit of the reality taught by himself [is] caused by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others. Thus [it is said].
Because the path to liberation is supreme, it bestows the enjoyments of heaven and other realms while one remains [in the world];
nor is it composed of human words by seers, nor likewise is it divine.
The gods did not disregard the word of Brahmā; nor did Viṣṇu disregard that of the lotus-born one; nor did Hari disregard that of Rudra; nor did Rudra disregard that which pertains to Śiva.
That which is to be sublated is higher and higher due to its superior distinction, while that which sublates is lower than the higher;
thus, the entire scripture is established in accordance with the Śiva-āgamas.
The Śiva-śāstra is not to be established by way of non-contradiction with other treatises or by way of agreement with them,
because it is that which establishes those very treatises.
"O Brahmins, for whatever scripture whatever extent of scope is intended, its authority shall extend only to that extent."
It is also indicated in the Sūtagītā: "The deity who is installed according to the method prescribed in the Tantras is worthy of being saluted, served, and worshipped by the followers of the Vedas."
But the king, most wise, should always establish all those who follow the Vedas as well as all those who follow the Tantras in their respective, unmixed states.
"A king should protect all [his subjects] with food, drink, clothing, and so forth.
Now, it was previously stated that the entire scripture, beginning with the Vedas, has Śiva as its author;
yet now it is said that other paths also have Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others as their authors.

It has been stated that [the Vedas] have Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others as their authors; this is a great contradiction. True. All scriptures, beginning with the Vedas, as well as the Śiva-śāstra, first emerge from the mouth of Śiva within Mahāmāyā in the form of *nāda* (sound-vibration); subsequently, they appear in the form of the arrangement of phonemes, words, and sentences.
There is no contradiction whatsoever in [the view] that this was composed by Śiva, both with and without a formal basis (sādhikaraṇa and niradhikaraṇa).
As it is stated in the venerable Kāmika:
"That which is worldly, that which is Vedic, and likewise that which is spiritual (ādhyātmika)..."
And the Atimārga, known as Mantra, is a single Tantra that appears in many forms.
The Siddhānta is the Mantratantra; the Atimārga is superior to that. The Ādhyātma is inferior to that, and the Vaidika is even lower than that.
The worldly [mantras] are inferior to the Vedic; the five deities beginning with Brahmā possess the forms of Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Mahāghora, Puruṣa, and Īśāna.
Each of these has five faces, and by them the worldly [mantras] and so forth were spoken;
from the Sadyojāta mantra emerged Brahmā, the beholder of all things.
By him indeed was the worldly scripture brought down into the mortal world:
grammar, poetics, etymology, and prosody.
The Bhārata, the science of astrology, the works of Vātsyāyana and others,
the science of longevity, the science of archery, and indeed the Ayurveda of trees;
Lokāyata, as well as Sāṃkhya, the doctrine of the Arhat,
Mīmāṃsā, Daṇḍanīti, and the worldly sciences such as Vārtā.
Viṣṇu, the lord of the mantras of the abodes, is the second Lord of Causes.
By him, the eighteen Purāṇas were indicated as Vedic.
Rudra emerged from the Terrible One (Ghora) and composed the Dharmaśāstra, Vedānta, Pāñcarātra, Bauddhaka, and the Adhyātma.
He composed the Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Sāṃkhya, and [Yoga] systems;
however, the Lord (Īśvara), having been born from Puruṣa, composed the Anima-path.
The Pañcārtha, the Lākula, and likewise the Pāśupata are considered [other systems].
Even the Blessed Lord Sadāśiva protected the Mantra and Tantra.
The words of Śiva are manifold: they are stated, prohibited, and then restated; they are both dependent and independent.
The entire [teaching] arising from the Ūrdhvasrotas was taught by Ananta and the others;
it was then spoken by the Supreme Lord to the high-souled Śrīkaṇṭha.
In the beginning, knowledge was twofold according to the distinction of its respective domains:
through the division of the higher and the lower, it reveals the nature of the Lord (pati) and the bound soul (pāśa).
The knowledge that reveals Śiva is remembered as the supreme Śivajñāna;
it is the higher realization beyond the Vedas and other sciences, which reveals the true nature of both the bound soul (paśu) and its fetters (pāśa).
Just as the eye has a different capacity at night than during the day for perceiving humans and their dwellings,
so too is knowledge of this kind— both supreme and non-supreme— of a distinct nature.
One should abandon a person who is devoted to the knowledge of astrology, whose mind is fixed on the Vedas and Purāṇas,
and who has exerted effort toward those goals established for perfected beings.
"One who, out of delusion, considers the Śiva-knowledge of the Kāmika and other scriptures to be equal to the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas— him one should avoid with great effort."
Furthermore, in that very same place: "The Gāruḍa, the Bhūtatantra, the Bhairava, the Vāma-mantra,
the Kāpāla, the Pāñcarātra, the Lākula, and the Kula-śāstra."
(p. 16) History and the six auxiliary sciences, as well as those known as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma [Vedas], the Atharvaveda, the Buddhist [scriptures], and the doctrine of the Arhat as well.
Because it arises from the scripture of the upward-stream (ūrdhvasrotas) and proceeds from the sequence of the faces of Aparaśānta,
the Śiva-knowledge beginning with the Kāmika is always the head of the Lord.
The other limbs of Maheśa, namely the heart, throat, and so forth,
have indeed been described here by Śambhu as the "prior positions" (pūrvapakṣa).
"In the definitive determination of things to be abandoned and things to be adopted from the perspective of ultimate reality,
having set all else aside, the Śiva-siddhānta is proclaimed."
Likewise, in the Mahābhārata, it is stated that the Vedas and other scriptures were composed by Śiva along with their authoritative commentaries:
"At the end of the age, the great sages [recovered] the vanished Vedas and Itihāsas..."
"They attained [their goals] through austerity, authorized by the Self-born One in the past," it is said.
And in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:
"Everything pertaining to the duties of those in the various stages of life (āśrama) here is established by the sacred tradition (āmnāya)."
These two were previously ordained by Brahmā, acting in accordance with my very command.
But that dharma of the Grandfather (Brahmā) involves many rites requiring great wealth;
it is not characterized by an abundance of results relative to the suffering and exertion involved.
By means of that great dharma, having attained faith which is very difficult to find,
those who possess the marks of the stages (varṇin) approach me, having no other refuge.
For their sake, by an easy path, I have established the conduct of the social classes and stages of life for the attainment of dharma, pleasure, wealth, and liberation.
"In that regard, only those of my own [disciples] among the social classes who possess devotion have the qualification, and not others; such is my final command."

Therefore, it is said that *tantra* refers to those humans for whom the path of the Vedas (*śruti*) has fallen away; *tantra* is not the *Śivāgama*. Furthermore, their study of the Śiva-āgamas is stated in the *Sambhava-kāṇḍa* of the Skanda Purāṇa: "In the meantime, O Lord, on Mount Kailāsa, the silver mountain..."
[It was taught] to Sanaka and the other lords of sages, in accordance with the meaning of the three categories.

It should be understood by the wise that the *Vāma*, *Ādi-tantra*, and others were created by Rudra through Māyā, impelled by the illustrious Īśvara, who is characterized by the feet of Śambhu. As it is stated in the *Kāmika*:

Likewise, in whatever manner, even though there is a difference in the nature of the general and the particular, the attainment of liberation without doubt exists through both the Vedāntic and Siddhāntic paths. As it has been said:

Both attain the exceedingly rare state of union (sāyujya) through both paths—

Having established the disciple in the center of the pavilion,

the power of Śambhu falls intensely upon that mass of consciousness.

A certain secret portion regarding the manner of the descent of power (śaktipāta) has not been stated by me,
both because of its secrecy and for fear of contradicting the King.

In this regard, too, the distinction is as follows: the power (*śakti*), being that which accomplishes the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā-karma*), falls first in a general form; subsequently, during the rite of initiation, it falls in a specific form, being directly of the nature of initiation itself. Thus it falls.
[Śakti: "Therefore, the destruction of impurity does not occur through the Vedic path;
rather, liberation itself is attained through initiation according to the path taught in the Śaiva Āgamas."

By the command of the Goddess, [the disciple] gradually burns away ignorance, which consists of impurity and delusion. Following initiation, the knowledge born from the Vedānta statements takes the form of self-knowledge and so forth, concerning the Self within the Self, with respect to the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth and ending with primordial nature (prakṛti).

The knowledge born of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) gradually burns away [the ignorance]. Subsequently, the knowledge born of the words of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), which has as its object the categories beginning with *rāga* and ending with *śiva*, likewise gradually burns away the ignorance born of *māyā*. The essential meaning is that, having reached the world-level (*bhuvana*) of the principle of the Person (*puruṣatattva*), one enjoys great enjoyment.

This has been stated in the *Sarvajñānottara* and other texts: "That which belongs to the followers of the Jina is characterized by darkness (*tāmasa*), while that of the proponents of Brahman is characterized by the Person (*pauruṣa*)."
The unreal has no being; the real never ceases to be.
Therefore, this doctrine of a single self is imagined by those of deluded intellect; thus do those possessed by the obsession of non-duality prattle, even as they are being shown compassion.
Those who, relying on the strength of non-duality, behave without restraint, are awakened by their gurus, who bestow the established doctrines and scriptures.
"For those who are established in non-duality, there is dissolution into the principle of the *puruṣa*;
for it is said that the knowers of Vedānta, the Sāṃkhyas, and the yogins are all situated in the *puruṣa*.

The Gāruḍa, the Bhairava, the Vāma, the Bhūtatantra, and the Yāmala.

They firmly established [this] by the path taught in the Āgamas;

The great city of Puṇḍarīka is the place that bestows the perfection of asceticism.

In the Śiva Purāṇa, in the section on the Greatness of Viriñci: "There was one named Śivanāyaka, a leader among the Brahmins devoted to Śiva,
who knew the meaning of the Kāmika and other Āgamas, and was like Maheśvara himself."
In the Śiva Purāṇa, in the section on the Greatness of Kālahasti: "Having bathed in the Suvarṇamukharī and recited the mantras according to the Jāpāgama, that brāhmaṇa,
with a tranquil soul, performed the rite of expiation."
One should worship the Lord according to the tantra, [saying] "May the barley-grains increase in the grove of asceticism.
In the *Śaivapurāṇa*, in the *Puṇḍarīkamāhātmya*:
"He who, having written the Śiva-scripture, gives it to a Śiva-yogi..."
Endowed with fierce devotion, one shall attain union with Śiva.

"The lord of the earth, having summoned the best of the twice-born created by Śiva— who were devoted to residing on the banks of the Gaṅgā— for the purpose of worshipping the Great Liṅga..."

Furthermore, in that same [text]:
"One should perform the consecration along with a great festival, using the waters of the Gaṅgā-tīrtha well-filled in golden jars, according to the rites prescribed in the Śivāgamas."
In the *Kuleśvara-vaibhava* section of the *Vedāraṇya-māhātmya*: "They worshipped with reverence, according to the path taught in the *Āgamas*,

The etymological definition of the word *āgama* and other terms has been stated by Aṃśumat and others:
"It has come (*āgata*) from the mouth of Śiva and gone (*gata*) into the mouth of the Daughter of the Mountain;

That by which reality is approached is traditionally known as *āgama*;
from that [source], one obtains exceedingly vast meanings based upon reality and mantra.

It would be useless;

since knowledge and the like lack autonomy, knowledge and so forth are a means to liberation only as constituent parts of initiation (*dīkṣā*), and not otherwise. As it has been said: "Its status as a constituent part [of that] is by means of that."
By that [rite], it becomes an ancillary to that [initiation];
thus, that initiation becomes possessed of its constituent parts, except for the one supreme Śiva-initiation which is accompanied by the leaf [of the *sapatra*] and is unimpeded.
One is not liberated through knowledge, nor through yoga, nor even through conduct;
for even there, the efficacy of knowledge and the other factors is not found to exist.

For children, the ignorant, the elderly, women, those addicted to sensual pleasures, and likewise the sick, there is no liberation through knowledge and the like; therefore, initiation alone is the liberator.
Even in the statement that "liberation comes from knowledge alone," the word "knowledge" (jñāna) has as its meaning initiation (dīkṣā) and so forth.
As it is said in the *Suprabheda*:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the section on knowledge (jñānapāda) in brief."
Listen now with a one-pointed mind to the creation of Śiva at the beginning of that.
O child, knowledge proceeds for the destruction of fatigue,
for the elimination of the succession of paths, and for the manifestation of Śiva.
Ignorance is said to be like darkness, knowledge is said to be like a lamp, and the object of knowledge is declared to be like the sun; afterwards, knowledge itself perishes.
Having severed the nets of bonds, initiation and so forth are called knowledge;
through knowledge, the wise one transcends the state of being a bound soul, a bond, and a lord.
(29) "But by knowledge alone is the attainment of liberation; there is no doubt in this regard.
And initiation (*dīkṣā*) is [effected] through the mere mental activity of the rites of worship, fire-offerings, and so forth, as manifested in the ritual act of initiation.
She is said to possess initiation and knowledge, and she brings about the perfect awakening to reality.
That which possesses sacrifice and fire, and arises from skill in ritual action, is "possessing action" (kriyāvatī);
it is manifold, being both seedless (nirbījā) and with seed (sabījikā).
In the Kālottara [Tantra] it is said:
"Initiation (dīkṣā) is declared to be 'actional' (kriyāvatī) for the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa;
furthermore, it is declared to be threefold as 'pertaining to the Hotṛ priest' (hautrī)."
In the Vāmana [Tantra], it is stated in the Śivāgama: "Initiation is taught by Śiva, the Supreme Self, as being threefold: namely, the Śāmbhavī, the Śāktī, and the Māntrī."
With the vision of the knowledge of reality, the Guru [perceives] from the tip of the nose up to the trident;
by the mere sight of the Guru, or by touch, or even by conversation, [the disciple attains realization].
In this context, that initiation which immediately brings about the destruction of the bonds is called Śāmbhavī; it is further divided into two types.
It is classified as "intense" and "more intense" according to the degree of exhaustion of the fetters;
that which results in immediate liberation is considered the more intense.
But the intense initiation pertaining to Śakti, which possesses knowledge, enters the body of the disciple and completely purifies his merit and sin while he is still alive.
By the Guru, through the path of yoga and with the eye of knowledge,
the initiation consisting of mantra and ritual action is performed, preceded by the preparation of the sacrificial pit and the pavilion.
The Guru should perform the external rite very slowly and gradually;
he should purify the disciple through either knowledge or ritual action.
"He who acts otherwise out of delusion perishes as one of evil intellect.
Thus it is said: "One is called Jñānavatī (the Knowledge-possessing), and the second is Kriyāvatī (the Action-possessing)."
Having extracted and stated this again in the *Śrīmac-Cintya-viśva-sādākhyam*:
"Thus, one who has successfully completed the initiation consisting of mantra-rituals is the most excellent in qualities;
he alone is qualified for the initiation of yoga, and no other."
Likewise, for disciples who have been previously initiated,
the supreme [initiation] is the threefold Śāmbhava, which arises from Śakti and consists of the Praṇava.
"The Śāktī and Śāmbhavī initiations are performed by you and me;
however, the Āṇava initiation is performed by others according to the distinctions of 'dull,' 'intense,' and so forth"—thus it has been stated.

Furthermore, even without the initiation of ritual action (kriyādīkṣā), [liberation occurs] through other gurus who possess the power of yoga, provided the disciple is either extremely ripe [for grace] or extremely destitute.

The teachers maintain that for an initiation (*dīkṣā*) performed through rituals deficient in mantras and so forth, either the Śākta or the Śāmbhava [initiation] should be performed, with one intervening between the other;
even by teachers who are yogis having practiced in some manner, there must be the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of mantras and rituals. (p. 31)

Because of the principle that "for one who has been initiated by a ritual initiation (kriyādīkṣā) complete with all its primary and secondary limbs, there is no possibility of performing [the rite] again," this very [initiation]— by virtue of being an ancillary to the ritual initiation— effects the immediate extraction of the Prāsāda mantra recited in unison, thereby bringing about the emergence of the sixfold qualities (ṣāḍguṇya) through the union with Śiva.

The meaning also flashes forth within that the Śākta and Śāmbhavī [initiations], which consist of the mantras of those [respective levels] and bring about the manifestation of one's own Śiva-nature, are condensed together as auxiliary causes.
One who is devoid of these three types of initiation is a *paśu* (bound soul). As it has been said:
A Brahmin who upholds the four Vedas but is devoid of Śiva-initiation is like the water of the Bhāgīrathī in the vessels of wicked Cāṇḍālas.
A Śūdra who is equal to ten million Brahmins and endowed with the initiation of Śiva is rare;
the knowledge of Śiva is very difficult to attain, and its practice is even more difficult to attain.
Knowing this to be very difficult to attain, one should practice devotion toward Śiva.
Thus ends the greatness of Śiva-initiation.
Next is the majesty of the devotees of Śiva; thereafter, the Śiva-śāstra is to be studied only by those of the four castes who have been initiated with the initiation of Śiva.
This is stated in the Suprabheda:
Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! That which you have requested is this Śuddhaśaiva Tantra; it must not be given away, nor should it be made public.
This should be heard only by one who is initiated, wise, and devoted to Śiva;
indeed, its proclamation elsewhere is not praised.
Through initiation, one should lead the four types of Śuddhaśaivas to Śiva;
now hear how they all conduct themselves according to the path of worldly custom.
Studying and teaching, performing sacrifices and officiating at sacrifices,
as well as whatever wealth is given dedicated to Śiva— these indeed constitute true giving.
"Then, the acceptance [of gifts] from him is said to be his sixfold duty, for the wise and pure Śaiva who is endowed with the true being of Śiva. Thus it is said.
In the *Makuṭa*:
"This unsurpassed tantra should be given to Śiva-yogins who have been initiated into Nirvāṇa; however, it must not be given to others."
And in the *Kāñcīpuramāhātmya*:
"A Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the Vedas, a devotee of Śiva, one who has conquered his senses,
endowed with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, and devoted to the worship of Śiva."
One who is devoted to the thorough understanding of the meaning of the scriptures and follows the dharma of Śiva—
whether he be a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra born of inverse-caste unions.
Or else, one may directly take refuge in Āmreśa, which arose in the natural order,
with devotion and according to one's means, by means of houses, fields, wealth, and so forth.
One should cause [the disciple] to dwell in the supreme state through devotion to the lotus-feet of the Guru;
the fruit that is proclaimed for the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the deities is attained thereby.
"Having obtained that entire fruit, one is liberated from the ocean of existence. Thus it is said in the Śaiva Purāṇa:
"Indeed, this [knowledge] should be given to a devotee of Śiva who has studied the Śiva-śāstras..."
"O best of sages, it is to be revealed to one who has been purified by the Śiva-initiation.
Thus it was stated by the venerable teacher Rāmakaṇṭha in his commentary on the *Kiraṇatantra*.
From this very fact, it is understood that he had successfully received the initiation of liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*).
Having begun by stating that "those who have not been initiated have no qualification for hearing [the scripture]," he will say, "all men having attained this...
Here, the word "all" refers to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, Mlecchas, and so forth; indeed, even these are qualified for the Śruti, because the context concerns the qualification of Garuḍa.

It has been explained that this is because the meaning of the word *sarva* (all) is not fixed; however, it must not be recited by those who have not received initiation (*dīkṣā*). As it is said in the *Kāmika*:
If Brahmins and members of the other three castes who are devoid of initiation, as well as those of Śūdra birth,
should study the Śiva-śāstra, the kingdom and its ruler will perish.
In the *Cintyaviśva*: "One who has not been initiated as a Brahmin or others should not write down the knowledge of Śiva;
moreover, one must especially not study it in the presence of one who is uninitiated."
In the Vīratantra: "It should be heard by those who have received the initiation into the channels (nādī), but it must not be given nor revealed.
It should indeed be given to disciples; I shall tell you this in brief."
And elsewhere it is said:
"A wise man should never, with effort, cause a bound soul (paśu) to write the knowledge of Śiva; nor should he engage in study in the presence of bound souls."
Even among the four castes, only those who have been initiated are superior. As it is stated in the Śiva Purāṇa:
"The Śūdra-hood of the Śūdra has departed, and the twice-born status of the Brāhmaṇa [has likewise vanished];
through connection with the Śiva-saṃskāra, no distinction of caste exists."
One who has been born through the initiation of Śiva should not contemplate his previous birth;
for when the Liṅga is firmly established, there is no longer any perception of prior existence.
In the Śivadharmottara:

Regarding the obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites, it has been well said by me that whatever ritual is situated within a single temple must be performed by a single preceptor.
The son or grandson of this teacher, his kinsman,
those initiated by him, or men who follow out of fear of his command— these are the ones who uphold [the tradition].
Those born in the original Śaiva lineage— whether Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, as well as those of the anuloma [castes] such as Gandharvas, dancers, and so forth— [are the recipients].
If the daughters of Rudra, who are my servants and the executors of my commands,
perform an action, that action shall be considered as performed by the Preceptor himself.
In the *Sūkṣma* [Tantra],
the rites of installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) and consecration (*sthāpanā*) and so forth are to be performed by an *Ādiśaiva*.
All those beginning with the *Anuśaiva* follow this sequence respectively in matters concerning their own personal practice (*ātmārtha*).
The initiate, the spiritual son, the practitioner, and the bearer of the form—
if they have gone to another country, they should act according to the command of the Guru.
If an obstacle should arise during another ritual performed through yoga, even if the preceptor is devoid of qualities,
it must be carried out by his son or disciple with his permission.
When there is a contradiction regarding the non-performance [of a rite] by the Guru due to a specific cause, that action must nevertheless be performed by his disciple according to the scriptures.
In the *Kāmika*:
"That which has been proclaimed for a Brāhmaṇa who has taken refuge in Śiva in the Śiva-āgama does not apply to the three [castes] beginning with the Kṣatriya for the sake of another."
In the Kāmika:
"Therefore, for the sake of others and for one's own sake, the ritual bathing for one's own benefit must be performed by a Śiva-brahmin; for that of others, it is indeed only for their own benefit."
If one should perform even a rite for the sake of another by omitting the king's portion, then the destruction of that kingdom will occur before long; of this there is no doubt.
In the Vīratantra:
"He who is born into the lineage of the Ādiśaiva is indeed called a *deśika* (preceptor).
By the Ādiśaiva, everything from the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) down to the ritual worship (*arcana*) must be performed."
Furthermore, regarding one who would cause [the rite] to be performed otherwise for the purpose of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*),
it is stated in that very same [text]:
"Those who are born in the lineages of those sages as Śiva-brahmins..."
They do not undergo initiation again; if it were to be performed, it would be fruitless.
Regarding the cause:
thereafter, the most excellent preceptor should conduct a festival for up to seven days,
or he may conduct a festival for even a single day.
From the commencement until the very end, if it should thus be the case that [the teacher] is present only in part,
then in the absence of the Ācārya, one should have it performed by the Mūrtipa.
One should cause all the implements of the sacrifice to be given to the preceptor (deśika).
Elsewhere it is said:
"One born in the lineage of the primordial Śaivas who has been consecrated by the initiation of Śiva..."
Born from the five objects of the senses, he was devoted to the performance of Śiva’s rites.
Having approached such a guru, one should perform the rites of installation and so forth;
such individuals are declared to be image-keepers (mūrtipas), and they should be brought to the sacrificial rite of homa.
In the *Kāmika*:
"The linga that is installed by Śiva-brahmins according to the sequence of the Siddhānta scriptures and other scriptures is of a dual nature."
For the prosperity of the king, the village, and the sacrificer,
a devotee of Śiva (śaiva) shall be the presiding authority over all matters, both in his own domain and elsewhere.
All those excellent twice-born householders who follow the Śaiva systems—
the Yāmala, the Māntratantra, the Kāpāla, and the Pāñcarātra— [are included].
Whether in the Buddhist or the Arhat (Jaina) traditions, or even in the Vaidika (Hindu) and other paths, according to the methods prescribed by their respective scriptures.
The Śaivas perform initiation and so forth, as well as the installation of their liṅgas and other rites.

Thus, it has been demonstrated that there are scriptural statements prohibiting the performance of worship for the sake of others by those Brāhmaṇas who belong to the lineage of Śiva (sāntānika-śiva) and who are worthy of worship by all castes. (p. 57)

Nevertheless, in certain works such as the *Suprabheda* and the *Ajita-āgama*, the worship for the sake of others (*parārthapūjā*) is somehow established for those great Śaivas who have been initiated into Śiva and whose minds are drawn by an excellence of devotion.
As stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"Because they are brought about by initiation (*dīkṣā*), they are therefore proclaimed as 'anuśaiva' (post-initiatory Śaiva)," beginning with these words.
Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, one should especially perform worship;
this is declared in the Śiva-āgama to be the duty of a Brāhmaṇa who has taken refuge in Ajita-Śiva.
Furthermore, for the three classes beginning with the Kṣatriya, worship performed for the sake of others is not [permitted].
In the *Hālāsyamāhātmya*:
"Brahmins who are devoid of initiation are unworthy of worshipping that Great Liṅga;
likewise, even Kṣatriyas must be initiated."
They all had it performed by various other Brahmins;
elsewhere it is said:
"In their midst, those worshippers, having again received initiation into the Śaiva [tradition]..."
"Indeed, these twice-born ones are worthy of worship by you for the sake of accomplishing your own and others' welfare."
(p. 58) Therefore, the distinction here is as follows:

worship is twofold, namely Vaidiki (Vedic) and Śaivī (Śaiva). Among these, although the Śaiva form of worship for the sake of others is said to be described among the Vaidikas according to the method previously stated, [it is distinct].

Although the ritual of worship (*arcana*) intended for those seeking liberation through the initiation of maturation (*paripākadīkṣā*) belongs exclusively to the great sages and great Śaivas who have been initiated into Śiva as part of their worship, and the supreme worship for the sake of others (*parārthapūjā*) is likewise exclusively Vedic; nevertheless,
it must be performed by those following the Vedic tradition alone according to the method prescribed in the *Bodhāyana-sūtra*.

This applies only to those who have received Śiva-initiation (śivadīkṣā) in some manner according to the methods taught in the Vedic Pāśupata and other systems, because they are not devoid of the Śiva-initiation prescribed in the Śiva-āgamas;
by no means does it apply to those who are entirely uninitiated.
This is because rituals beginning with land-plowing and ending with consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), festivals,
and expiations depend upon the Śiva Āgama; and since those who have not received initiation lack authority regarding the Śiva Āgama,
its dependence [on that scripture] is declared in the *Sūta-saṃhitā* and other Purāṇas as a means of supplementing the Veda.
O Brahmins, at the outset, with focused minds, they should worship the Śivaliṅga, which is characterized by the definitions proclaimed in the scripture (āgama), even if it be out of a lack of faith.
In the *Brahmottara-khaṇḍa*: "The wise one should consecrate the seat according to the procedure taught in the Āgamas.
And in the *Smṛti*:
Even some knowers of the Vedas, desiring the fruit thereof, attain perfection by worshipping the gods through the path of Tantra.

(p. 59) Likewise, in the Vedic *Parārthamīmāṃsā*, the venerable Āpaduddhāraṇadīkṣitas also indicated the necessity of the Śiva-āgamas and Śiva-initiation (*śivadīkṣā*). This is because [the Vedic path] proceeds in its entirety only for those who are qualified for the most excellent primary rituals (*pradhānaprakṛṣṭakarman*).

One who prioritizes truth should not perform such an action; for an action performed in that manner produces all the faults described. Furthermore, according to the logic of Mīmāṃsā, among various forms of worship, the Śaiva Tantric worship is the primary one. Among those, it is the primary [worship] for those who possess the primary qualification.
In the absence of Śiva-brāhmaṇas, the king should somehow have the Vedic worship of Śiva performed by a Vedic priest. The Paurāṇika method for the supreme Vedic worship is now set forth.
Due to the defects of the Kali age, great delusion will arise among mortals;
there will not be pure devotion to the path of the Vedas in any way whatsoever.
Those who constantly place their faith in paths outside the Vedas will become short-lived and especially impoverished.
Afflicted by mental and physical ailments, weapons, and swords, as well as by tigers, thieves, and the like,
they have abandoned the conduct of their castes and stages of life due to the total loss of specific means of protection.
Again and again, through no choice of their own, they shall be born in all wombs;
yet they shall increase the kingdom and the realm for me, who am characterized as described above and accompanied by Ambā.
Having installed [the image] on the riverbank using only the *praṇava* (Om),
one will certainly become a sovereign ruler through divine offerings such as perfumes and flowers.
One should construct a wonderful temple provided with walls and gate-towers;
one should offer dance, song, and so forth, as well as pure rice, at the three junctions of the day.
Having installed Ṣaṇmukha in the northwest corner and Vināyaka in the southwest,
one should worship them daily for the increase of the king and the kingdom.
The twice-born should perform worship for the prosperity of the king and the kingdom;
by worshipping me there, the king attains victory.
Endowed with long life and health, he shall become liberated;
and his enemies, O Goddess, will perish for the king—of this there is no doubt.
Through my worship, may the kingdom everywhere and at all times abound with wealth and grain; may there be prosperity in every respect at every season.
"All human beings will be devoted to the conduct prescribed for their respective castes and stages of life;
of this there is no doubt. Therefore, one should worship me there.
Thus, even for those Brāhmaṇas other than the Śiva-Brāhmaṇas...
It should be understood that even the worship for the sake of others, though spoken of, is only in a figurative sense.
Thus ends the greatness of the Śaiva teacher.

Now, the procedure for the Śaiva preceptors of the four castes is stated. As it is said in the Śaiva Purāṇa: "Those belonging to the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, who are fully endowed with the Śiva-śāstra and are averse to the Paśu-śāstra, are proclaimed as preceptors."
In the *Kāmika*:
"For the installation of a mobile liṅga for one's own sake, there are these eight;
however, for a Śūdra, in the case of a Śūdra-initiation and for one's own sake, it is that which is designated as 'mobile'."
In the *Suprabheda*:
"Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those born of the Śūdra caste—
these are to be known as teachers, and never others."
In that very same *Jātinirṇaya*:
"Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are indeed proclaimed;
one should appoint these four castes to the office of teacher."
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are pure are the practitioners (*sādhakas*);
and the teachers (*ācāryas*), O Six-faced One, follow the sequence according to their own respective castes."
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"The status of an *ācārya* is prescribed for these ten classes: the four beginning with the Brahmin, and the six born in the natural order (*anuloma*) and so forth."
A Brahmin, having bowed to all castes, is the teacher of three; a Kṣatriya, of three;
and a Vaiśya or Śūdra, of two or one respectively—the knower of the purpose of vision and action should thus initiate them.
The Brāhmaṇa is traditionally held to be the perpetual benefactor of all castes;
among his own caste, there are three types of teachers, while the others, such as kings and so forth, are considered inferior.
Likewise, in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*:
"In this [system], the status of being a teacher is declared for all four castes;
among the four beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, the twice-born is considered the one who bestows grace."
A Kṣatriya [is purified] by three [initiations], a Vaiśya by two, while a Śūdra who is not born from a womb [is purified] by one;
thus, grace should be bestowed by all four types of teachers.
In the *Kiraṇa*, Garuḍa asks: "Tell me, which among the four letters in the middle possesses weight (*gurutva*)? Īśvara replies:
In this world, the status of being a teacher for all four castes is declared;
among the four beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, the twice-born is considered the benefactor.
"A Kṣatriya [is born] from three [castes], a Vaiśya from two, but a Śūdra is not born from a womb.
Furthermore, in the *Kāmika*:
"The triad beginning with the Nitya [rites] should be performed by means of the four [initiations], according to the investigation [of the disciple]."
Likewise, a Śūdra, having abandoned the Vaiśvadeva rite and the Sandhyā prayers consisting of the Self...
In the *Kālottara*: "One who has been thus consecrated— whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya,
or even a Śūdra— is qualified for the installation of images and other such rites."

Now, it might be argued that the statements demonstrating the gravity of the fourth subject matter (the fourth *viṣaya*) concern only the lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika*) Śūdra, and not the householder (*gṛhastha*). As it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
Even a Śūdra may be the installer [of a liṅga] during the initiation of a Śūdra, for his own sake, in the case of a liṅga known as "movable" (cala),
or in the case of a Bāṇaliṅga or a Kṣaṇika-liṅga, provided he is a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika).
Even for a Śūdra householder, there is fitness for only these eight daily rites;
he is unfit even for the consecration ceremony (abhiṣeka), let alone for the installation (sthāpana) and other such rituals.
This statement is true only in certain cases where it depends upon the intention of the listener;

otherwise, according to the maxim "we shall be many," it is indeed meaningless. And thus say those who know the nature of sentences: "In a conflict between properties of equal force, that which pertains to the majority shall prevail."
Regarding commonality with the world:
one should abandon an individual for the sake of the family; one should abandon the family for the sake of the village;
one should abandon the village for the sake of the country; and one should abandon the entire earth for the sake of the Self, and so forth.

Regarding the avoidance of contradictions with the Purāṇas, this same principle was stated by the venerable Skandarāta: "That which is contradicted by a Vedic [text] should be set aside; that which is connected with it should be led forward;
the small should be led by the great; and likewise, one should follow the conduct of the virtuous, like a traveler on a path."

And as for the phrase "and another": the status of the Śūdra householder as a Guru is already established. Furthermore, statements regarding the inferiority of the *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong celibate), such as "the *naiṣṭhika* is to be known as lower," are also to be resolved by the aforementioned reasoning.
As it is said in the *Parākhyatantra*:

p. 64) "The householder is declared to be the best among all social classes (varṇas) and the preceptor; the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) should be known as inferior, and the materialist (bhautika) especially so."
In the Kālottara it is stated: "In this Siddhānta, the status of an Ācārya has been established by Śiva for all four castes, as well as for those bearing sectarian marks (liṅgins) and householders."
In the *Uttarakāmika*:
"The office of preceptor specifically belongs to householders of the four castes;
or else, the office of preceptor specifically belongs to celibate students."
In the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*:
"Listen, O Six-faced One, to the reality of how enjoyment and liberation truly exist:
the supreme teacher is of two kinds—the celibate student (*brahmacārī*) and the householder (*gṛhastha*)."
Both of these are qualified for initiation (dīkṣā) and installation (pratiṣṭhā);
however, they are [intended] for those whose sole aim is liberation and whose minds are turned away from worldly prosperity.
The celibate student (brahmacārī) is to be known as the teacher for [those of] both types, and the householder is the teacher for those of both types as well;
however, for those other than the householder, there is no entitlement to enjoyments.
"Therefore, a leader should be made a guru by those seeking both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Likewise, regarding the lineage:
"The householder is superior in knowledge; the celibate student (brahmacārin) would be inferior."
In the *Suprabheda*:
"The householder is to be known as the highest, as is the material celibate (*bhautika-brahmacārin*).
In the *Vīra-tantra*:
A householder who maintains the lineage is the best; in its absence, any householder [is acceptable].

"The material celibate (bhautika-brahmacārī) is the teacher for householders; the lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) is considered to be [the teacher] for those seeking both worldly enjoyment and liberation, respectively. Thus it is stated in the *Kiraṇa*.
The householder is declared to be the lineage-guru, the most excellent of teachers;
one should know the householder to be supreme, or else the celibate student (brahmacārin).
"A householder is the best of teachers for the attainment of both enjoyment and liberation.
As stated in the *Kāmika*: "Those such as Kauśika and others who were initiated in the period immediately following the [cosmic] emanation..."
By means of Śiva, those twice-born ones born of that lineage shall become Śaivas who ensure the continuity of their progeny.
The preceptor of one's own lineage is the best; in his absence, a householder, a student of the elements, or a celibate student may serve as the instructor for householders.
The lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) should be among those who are lifelong celibates; he is considered [the teacher] according to the sequence of enjoyment and liberation.
For the sake of attaining both enjoyment and liberation, the householder is desired as the guru.
In that very same [text], it says:
"O Brahmin, one should then consecrate the twice-born in the northern direction of the Great City;
the Kṣatriyas in the eastern direction, and the Vaiśyas in the direction of Yama (the south)."
"But all Śūdras [should be placed] in the western direction, or all [castes] situated as appropriate.
Even one devoid of all auspicious marks is accepted as a Guru if he possesses knowledge.
He who discriminates between caste and non-caste would be a sinner.
Thus ends the greatness of the Śaiva Ācāryas of the four castes.
Regarding the procedure for renunciation for the four castes, it is stated in the *Cintyaviśva*:
"Ascetics are to be known as threefold: the practitioner of austerities (*tapasvin*), the learned one (*vidvas*), and [the third]."
The wise man is said to be of three kinds; their characteristics are now described.
"O observer of excellent vows, for one who is established in austerity and is an ascetic,
his conduct is such that he must never study, nor form any resolve, nor listen to anything at all."
He who reveals the knowledge should not engage in gathering disciples;
he should not speak in Sanskrit, nor carry a staff, nor a water-pot.
Having worshipped the linga and the dice, endowed with mere devotion,
he should remain alone at the foot of a tree or in a forest devoid of people.
Filled with fear of people, he should live with his arm as a pillow;
let his clothing be whatever it may be, and likewise his food and drink.
Using his hands as a bowl and his stomach as a vessel, living on food obtained through begging—one who is thus described is a true ascetic; such a practitioner becomes renowned by that name.
O Nandikeśvara, the conduct of both the learned man and the ascetic consists likewise of teaching,
studying, listening, and reflecting.

These four [stages] belong especially to that wise man; however, there is a distinction between the learned man and the ascetic: for the former, there is exposition, while for the latter, there is reflection.

One who is endowed with the consecration of a true preceptor is designated as a "learned one" (vidvat). Among the Śaivas within the four stages of life (āśrama), three types of ascetics (yati) are proclaimed.
There is indeed a distinction among the stages of life (āśramas), but no difference in their ultimate goal (niṣṭhā).

In the Sūta-saṃhitā, the Kiraṇa-tantra, and other texts, the names and the procedures for digging, burning, and so forth should be understood through various methods; these are also found in the Suprabheda.
The four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, who originated from Kaśyapa and others,
were appointed to their respective offices by the grace of the Supreme Lord.
I shall briefly explain the *gocara* and the *gotrasūtra*:
the *gocara* is indeed the sign of Śiva, while the *gotra* consists of one's own group of sages.
p. 68) Thus, the Sūtra concerning the conduct of the Śaivas is declared in sequence:
Śiva, the Topknot (śikhā), likewise Light (jyotis), and the Sāvitrī; these are the spheres of activity.
These are the four names of the Śaivas in the teaching of Śiva;
their sphere of perception and their fourfold insignia are as follows.
Kāśyapa, Kauśika, Bhāradvāja, and Gautama—
these four types of sages are to be known as those proclaimed here.
For the vow is said to be of two kinds: general and specific.
[The specific vows pertain to] the student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant.
For thus the four stages of life (āśramas) are enjoined by the general injunction; and this Śivāgama is the equalizer of the four spheres of experience.
And in the Kālottara:
"Śiva, Śikhā, Jyotis, and Sāvitrī—this is the tetrad.
The Śaiva-kula is born from Śiva; the Śikhā[-kula] is born from Śakti."
From the *bindu* arises the family of *jyotis*, and from the *nāda* arises the *sāvitra*;
at the time of initiation, when the mantra dissolves into Śiva and the other [deities].
The four families (kula) arise in sequence by virtue of their respective gateways;
this sequence should be understood as applying to the four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
Upon the arising of pure birth, that common lineage which was established would perish. In the Kṛtayuga, the Brāhmaṇa renunciant is supreme; in the Tretāyuga, the Kṣatriya renunciant is supreme;
in the Dvāparayuga, the Vaiśya renunciant is supreme; and in the Kaliyuga, the Śūdra renunciant [is supreme]. (p. 69)
The passage beginning with "the best" (*śreṣṭha*) and so forth should be understood as it appears in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* and other texts.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*, it is said:
"There are only two [true] ascetics: the householder and the celibate student."
They are indeed benefactors of the world, not merely wandering mendicants or forest ascetics.
In the *Kālottara*:
"The status of being a Guru is never desired for forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) or ascetics (*yati*).
In the *Suprabheda*:

If it is asked: "Since there are prohibitive statements such as 'When these [ascetics] have abandoned the fire of the substance of existence (bhāvadravya), they are renunciants (saṃnyāsins); therefore, they are not qualified for initiation (dīkṣā) or the installation [of a deity] (sthāpana),' how can they speak of the status of renunciants as spiritual teachers (guru)? [The answer is: True. This refers to the practice known as the *āṇavī* [initiation].

Initiation is of two kinds: the Śāktī and the Śāmbhavī. Within that [latter], there certainly exists a certain degree of the status of a Guru, in some way and in some instances, regarding the Jñānavatī initiation. As it is said in the Sannyāsadīpikā:
For the Parahaṃsa ascetics and for those who have renounced all worldly ties (saṃnyāsins),
eligibility for the fire-rituals is not prescribed;
for these two, consecration is thus ordained without the performance of *homa*.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for Śaiva renunciation.
p. 70) The Procedure for the Authority to Perform Śiva Worship.
In the Raurava hell it is white in color; in the Vīci hell it is red for a Kṣatriya;
it is yellow for a Vaiśya, and black for the fourth [caste].
In the *Jñānasāra*: "White, red, yellow, and black—
these four colors are the sequence for the lingas of the four castes, beginning with the Brahmins."
Alternatively, that [liṅga] which is black in color may be suitable for all castes.
As stated in the *Kālottara*:
"Due to its lack of specific qualities, the black-colored [liṅga] bestows success among all castes."
In that very place:
"The black [liṅga] bestows the accomplishment of all goals and brings benefit to the four castes;
or else, for all people, the white Bāṇaliṅga grants liberation."
Regarding the subtle [forms]:
for a Brāhmaṇa it is eight-cornered, for a Kṣatriya it is six-cornered;
for a Vaiśya it should be four-cornered, and for a Śūdra it is indeed circular.
In all castes, the wise man should construct a circular pedestal (*pīṭha*).
As stated in the *Vidyāsārasaṃhitā*:
"The *ra*-liṅga shall grant all desired objects to Brāhmaṇas."
A liṅga made of gems bestows great sovereignty upon Kṣatriyas.
A golden liṅga indeed bestows great wealth upon Vaiśyas;
they know that a stone liṅga grants great sovereignty to Śūdras.
The crystal and the Bāṇaliṅga grant all desires to everyone;
however, for women, especially those with husbands, an earthen liṅga is recommended.
O you of excellent vows, for widows who have desisted from worldly life, there is the sequential practice of the *rasaliṅga* and so forth,
whether in childhood, youth, or old age.
A liṅga made of pure crystal indeed bestows immediate enjoyment upon women;
in the Aṃśumatī [tradition], Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and even Śūdras may be initiated.
One may perform worship for one's own sake, but not for the sake of others;
and especially so regarding the worship of women born of the four castes. Thus ends the rule concerning the qualification for Śiva-pūjā.
In the *Jñānapāda* of the *Suprabheda*, there is a statement explaining the fault of reviling Śiva and others:
"The theft of the property of the deity, the reviler of the Śiva-scriptures, the killer of one's father, the slayer of a Brahmin, and many others such as these. (p. 72)
Resorting to places of torment, they fall into the ocean of hell.
In the section on instruction:
"O twice-born ones, these six— Śambhu and the others, as well as the abodes of Śiva, the Vedas, the sacred ash, the rudrākṣa beads, and the Āgamas— are all auspicious."
Likewise, he who disparages the Śiva Purāṇas and other supreme texts concerning Śiva is called a fool and a traitor to Śiva.
Staying near one who reviles [the Lord], as well as hearing,
seeing, touching him, and conversing with him;
Hearing such words is likewise declared to be an offense against Śiva.
In the *Virūpākṣamāhātmya*, the first part of the essence of all Purāṇas beginning with the *Brahmāṇḍa*:
"The scripture of Śiva, the conduct of Śiva, the mantra of Śiva, and the exaltation of Śiva..."
The world of Śiva, the knowledge of Śiva, meditation on Śiva, and the worship of Śiva.
Those sinners who treat Śiva’s power, Śiva’s hymn, Śiva’s sacred field, and Śiva’s scripture as insignificant— may they be bound incessantly in the most intense [hell].
If he were to kill first the Śaivas, the Pāśupatas, the Kālāmukhas, and those who wear the skull-bowl, the entire world would have already been destroyed by that evil-minded one.
In the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa* of the *Skanda-purāṇa*, these are the words of Śiva addressed to Viṣṇu:
"Those lowest of men who revile others devoted to my hermitage—
the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas— who are protected by the armor of Śiva’s weapons."
O best of gods, they will undoubtedly become heretics;
for them, their asceticism, burnt offerings, recitations, ritual bathing, meditation, and worship [will be in vain].
Like an oblation poured into ashes, everything becomes fruitless for him who hates one devoted to my hermitage; he who hates that person hates Mādhava himself.
He who praises those who delight in my hermitage praises me, the stainless one;
they shall be capable of protecting those who fall into the ocean of hell.
In the *Svacchanda*: "O beloved, whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or others,
all of them possess equal dharma when united with the abode of Śiva."
All are said to wear matted locks, their bodies smeared with ashes;
all eat from a single row [of vessels], O fair-faced one.
Having mastered this mantra, one should certainly not disclose one's previous birth to the spiritual sons (putraka),
the practitioners (sādhaka), or even the initiates (samayin).
O Goddess, by uttering [the name] before one's birth, one becomes exempt from penance;
however, for Rudra it lasts for three days, and for Keśava for five days.
O Supreme Goddess, that [person] who [kills] Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras is cooked in hell for one half of his grandfather’s lifespan.
And all those who are established in the state of a hermitage abide in auspiciousness;
otherwise, those lowest of men perceive them according to their former nature.
They are cooked in hell for a period known as *sāda* for three years.
As stated in the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*:
"The fool who delights in reviling Śiva and who censures the scriptures of Śiva..."
Having seen no remedy for that anywhere even in any scripture by anyone, [he became despondent].
And in the Sūta-saṃhitā: "If the knowledge of Brahman exists in either a woman or a man,
there is never any [obligation] for them regarding the conduct prescribed for their caste and stage of life."
"O believers, he who abandons the knowledge of the Self—which is to be known along with one's caste and stage of life—is a deluded soul; [he is lost]. Thus it is stated in the *Manusmṛti*.
The triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes should be worn constantly by the twice-born and others;
[the merit] he attains is like the fruit of what has been given.

And in the *Vṛddhācalamāhātmya*: "Whether during a ritual bath, recitation, or fire-offering, on a specific lunar day, in the worship of a deity, or when performing initiation (*dīkṣā*) or ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), one who wears a rosary of rudrākṣa beads becomes sanctified."

Since lifespan, karma, and the entirety of Vedic injunctions have not yet reached their exhaustion, if their fruit were not to manifest, this [Veda] would be in vain; alas, this person would thus be both sinful and yet blameless.
O Aṃśumatī,
a Śrāddha performed without the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), an oblation (āhuti) without the triple mark,
and a gift (dāna) without the triple mark— these are proclaimed to be demonic (rākṣasa).
Therefore, it is certain that those men who are devoted to the specific practices proclaimed in the Śiva-āgamas attain abundant spiritual blessings.
Thus ends the Compendium on the Greatness of the Śivāgamas and Other Texts, composed by Jñānaprakāśa Guru, a resident of Śālivāṭipuram.
